title: Man. Post. Cap. II: strictissime poena — three conditions; Ursinus fiat iustitia
pass_a_gloss: Namely you establish that it is a penalty in the strictest and most proper sense so called, whose conditions are these. 1. The Law threatens it. 2. Justice requires that it be inflicted by the Judge. 3. The Judge inflicts it that justice may be done, or that justice may be satisfied. Thus Ursinus in the Catechetical Explanation. When he had objected to himself that God ought not to have punished the fault of Adam with such a penalty, he answered let justice be done and the World perish.
pass_b_english: On your account this is penalty in the tightest proper sense, and you put three marks on it. The Law must threaten it. Justice must demand that the Judge lay it on. The Judge must lay it on so justice is done—or so justice is satisfied. Ursinus, in the Catechetical Explanation, faced the objection that God should not have punished Adam with such a penalty, and answered: Let justice be done, though the world perish.
source_text: Nempe statuis esse poenam strictissime ac propriissime sic dictam, cujus hae sunt conditiones. 1. Lex eam comminatur. 2. Iustitia ut infligatur a Iudice exigit. 3. Iudex eam infligit ut fiat iustitia, sive ut iustitiae satisfiat. Itaque Ursinus in explicat. Catechet. Cum sibi objecisset non debuisse Deum culpam Adami tali poena punire, respondit fiat iustitia & pereat Mundus.
